title: Cloud & Infrastructure as Code
description: 25 lessons, three stage projects and a locally runnable practice kit covering Azure infrastructure decisions, Terraform concepts, policy and safe lifecycle review.
level: Foundations → intermediate practice with optional systems labs
prerequisites: Basic application, network and terminal concepts; earlier delivery, security and system-design paths are helpful.
Python 3.14+ for the offline lab. No cloud account, payment method or broker is required.
outcomes: Map Azure scope, identity and network responsibilities.
Review infrastructure desired state, dependencies and protected state.
Classify create/update/replacement/deletion and model cost arithmetic.
Run offline policy tests and inspect optional Azure Terraform schema validation.
Design credentialed delivery, data restoration, cost controls and verified teardown.
setup: Download the practice bundle and extract its flat files together.
From its folder run python infra_lab.py, then python -m unittest -v test_infra_lab.py.
Read README.md and workbook.md before optional external tooling. The verified baseline is local only.
nextSteps: Choose a disposable subscription scope deliberately; review costs, identity and cleanup before optional real cloud work.
Connect this work to the full-stack journey. Record which integration tests you ran and which still need a live environment.

lessons.title: 1. Cloud is a responsibility boundary
lessons.takeaway: Managed infrastructure still needs an application owner.

sections.title: Service models and responsibilities
paragraphs: Cloud services rent compute, storage, networking and managed capabilities through provider APIs. A service model determines which operating tasks the provider performs and which remain yours. Running an application on managed compute does not automatically configure authorization, protect application data, establish backups or enforce cost limits.

sections.title: Static versus private notebook needs
paragraphs: The notebook can remain a static GitHub Pages site. A future private full-stack notebook needs an API, identity, data store and operational owner. Choosing managed services changes the work required; it does not justify adding a cloud service to every feature.

quiz.question: Managed infrastructure still needs an application owner. Which decision follows?
options: Assign an owner to application security, data recovery and spending.
Assume a managed service makes the entire workload secure automatically.
Assume the provider's infrastructure backup proves the application's point-in-time recovery target.
quiz.explanation: Managed infrastructure shifts particular responsibilities rather than removing workload ownership.

exercise.prompt: List responsibilities for static hosting, a VM and a managed database. Name who patches the guest OS, grants application access, validates restores and responds to a leak. Treat the offline kit as design practice only.
checks: Compare guest OS responsibility for a VM versus managed service.
Name owners for application access and restore verification.
exercise.solution: Static hosting owns web asset delivery while the learner owns content and browser behavior. A VM adds guest OS patching and service operations. Managed databases reduce selected engine operations but retain application access, backup configuration and restore verification responsibilities. Assign an owner to leaks, identity and recovery instead of assuming a service model solves them.

lessons.title: 2. Azure tenant, subscription and resource group
lessons.takeaway: Verify identity, billing scope and ownership before a plan.

sections.title: Tenant, subscription and resource group
paragraphs: A tenant is an identity directory; a subscription is a resource and billing scope; a resource group organizes related resources. Region determines resource placement subject to service support. Names and labels cannot substitute for checking the actual subscription ID. Resource groups should have a lifecycle owner, purpose and expiry for temporary learning work.

sections.title: An explicit training scope
paragraphs: A developer belongs to two tenants and has access to a work and personal subscription. A familiar resource-group name can exist in the wrong subscription. The optional template requires an explicit `subscription_id` and declares a named training resource group and a storage account inside it. A separate apply would create both resources.

quiz.question: Verify identity, billing scope and ownership before a plan. Which decision follows?
options: Require explicit scope and lifecycle metadata before real provisioning.
Infer the target subscription from the current CLI default.
Use matching resource-group names as proof that two plans target the same subscription.
quiz.explanation: Ambient account defaults can drift; a deliberate scope check is a deployment prerequisite.

checks: Record explicit identity and subscription scope.
Distinguish a fictional fixture from a verified real deployment target.

A familiar name or current CLI default is insufficient scope evidence.

lessons.title: 3. Workload requirements and service selection
lessons.takeaway: Select services from workload constraints and reversible tradeoffs.

sections.title: Workload and recovery requirements
paragraphs: Start with users, data sensitivity, request pattern, recovery targets and deployment frequency. Compare static hosting, managed application compute and VMs. A container orchestrator is useful for some workloads but introduces extra operations. Define what must be measured rather than claiming a provider icon guarantees performance or availability.

sections.title: Static hosting versus managed compute
paragraphs: A personal notebook needs mostly cached static assets. A collaborative project adds authenticated writes and a database. For a training API, managed application compute can reduce OS work; Kubernetes can be a learning choice, but its cluster lifecycle is an additional responsibility.

sections.title: A small decision to try
paragraphs: An architecture decision record, or ADR, is a short explanation of the need, options, choice and reason to revisit it. For this exercise use 20 learners, occasional note writes and no custom operating-system packages. One learner maintains the app. All records are synthetic, and nothing is deployed by this exercise.

Compare managed application compute plus a data store with a VM hosting the API. List compute uptime, stored data, outbound transfer and logs as cost categories. Use categories only; the cost-control lesson handles estimates. A new requirement for a custom OS component would be a reason to reconsider the choice.

quiz.question: Select services from workload constraints and reversible tradeoffs. Which decision follows?
options: Document constraints and compare two viable service models.
Use Kubernetes for every workload because it appears advanced.
Select the cheapest compute line item and ignore database, egress and monitoring responsibilities.
quiz.explanation: Architecture should address stated needs and make its operational and financial costs visible.

exercise.prompt: For the 20-learner scenario, choose managed application compute or a VM. Give the constraint that drives your choice and one changed requirement that would make you reconsider.
exercise.solution: Managed application compute is a reasonable first choice because the app needs no custom OS and has one maintainer. The owner still handles application permissions and recovery. A required unsupported OS component could justify a VM and its added patching duties. A different choice needs an explicit constraint; no price is implied.
checks: Use the supplied workload and maintenance constraint.
Name a changed requirement that would reverse the decision.

lessons.title: 4. Choose a compute service
lessons.takeaway: Pick the most managed compute that still meets the workload's runtime, scaling and control requirements; each step down the list hands you more operating work.

sections.title: From virtual machines to functions
paragraphs: Azure offers a ladder of compute services. Virtual Machines give full control of the operating system, so you patch, harden and scale it yourself (lesson 1's responsibility boundary moves towards you). App Service runs web apps and APIs on a managed platform with deployment slots, TLS and built-in scale-out. Container Apps runs containers with HTTP and event-driven scaling, including scaling to zero, without managing a Kubernetes cluster. Azure Kubernetes Service gives a managed control plane, but you operate nodes, upgrades and cluster add-ons. Azure Functions runs short event-triggered code and bills per execution on consumption-style plans.

Start from the workload requirements of lesson 3: the runtime and dependencies, how load arrives (steady requests, bursts, queue messages, schedules), how long one unit of work runs, start-up latency tolerance, network isolation and the team's operating capacity. Move down to a less managed option only for a stated reason, such as a custom kernel module or a long-running stateful process.

sections.title: A decision for the notebook API
paragraphs: The table records one decision for a small notebook API and its nightly export job. It names the trigger that would reopen it, as lesson 3 recommends.
sections.example:
Workload                 Needs                                  Choice            Why not the others
Notebook API (HTTP)      container image, bursts, idle at night  Container Apps    VM: patching for no benefit; AKS: cluster ops
                                                                                   for one service; Functions: long requests
Nightly export (15 min)  scheduled, runs to completion           Container Apps    Functions: execution time limits on some plans
                         job, same image                                           and a second packaging model
Legacy reporting tool    needs a Windows service and a           Virtual Machine   requires OS-level installation
                         licensed driver
Reopen if: the platform needs service mesh or custom operators (consider AKS), or cold starts break the latency objective (set a minimum replica).

exercise.prompt: A webhook receiver gets about 200 requests a day in unpredictable bursts, each handled in under a second by a small Python function, and the team has no operations staff. Choose a compute service, state the requirement that decided it, and name one risk and its mitigation.
exercise.solution: Azure Functions on a consumption-style plan (or Container Apps scaled to zero): the load is rare, bursty and short, so per-execution billing and platform-managed scaling fit, and the team avoids patching. A VM or AKS would leave idle capacity and operating work. Risk: cold starts delay the first request after idle; mitigate by checking the webhook sender's timeout and retry policy, or keep one warm instance on a premium plan if the latency objective requires it. Also make the handler idempotent because senders retry.
checks: Ties the choice to load pattern, duration and operating capacity.
Explains why a less managed option adds unneeded work.
Names cold start (or another real risk) with a mitigation.

quiz.question: A service needs a custom kernel module on its hosts. Which compute option fits?
options: Azure Functions
App Service
Virtual Machines
quiz.explanation: Only a VM (or nodes you manage) gives operating-system control. Managed platforms do not let you load kernel modules.

lessons.title: 5. Choose managed databases and storage tiers
lessons.takeaway: Managed data services take over patching, backups and replicas, but you still choose the redundancy, recovery window and storage tier, and those choices set both cost and what you can recover.

sections.title: Managed databases and storage accounts
paragraphs: Azure SQL Database is a managed SQL Server engine: the platform patches it, takes automatic backups for point-in-time restore within a retention window you configure, and can add zone redundancy or readable geo-replicas. You still own the schema, queries, logins, firewall or private endpoint (lesson 6), and testing a restore. Other managed engines (Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Cosmos DB) follow the same split.

A storage account holds blobs, files, queues and tables. Its redundancy setting decides which failures it survives: locally redundant storage keeps three copies in one datacenter, zone-redundant storage spreads them across availability zones, and geo-redundant options copy asynchronously to a second region, so the latest writes can be lost on a regional failover. Redundancy is not a backup: a deleted or overwritten blob is deleted everywhere, so enable soft delete or versioning for that (lesson 23).

sections.title: Blob access tiers
paragraphs: Blob access tiers trade storage price against access price. Hot is cheapest to read; cool, cold and archive are cheaper to store but charge more to read and have minimum retention periods (30, 90 and 180 days) with early-deletion charges. Archive is offline: a blob must be rehydrated, which can take hours, before it can be read. Lifecycle management rules can move blobs between tiers by age.
With the invented rates below, rarely read exports are cheapest in archive, but heavy reads make hot the cheapest. Rehydration time, not only price, rules archive out for data a user may need today.
sections.example:
# Invented teaching rates per GB-month and per GB read; real prices vary by region and change.
TIERS = {
    'hot':     {'store': 0.020, 'read': 0.000, 'min_days': 0},
    'cool':    {'store': 0.010, 'read': 0.010, 'min_days': 30},
    'cold':    {'store': 0.004, 'read': 0.030, 'min_days': 90},
    'archive': {'store': 0.001, 'read': 0.020, 'min_days': 180},
}

def monthly(tier, stored_gb, read_gb):
    t = TIERS[tier]
    return stored_gb * t['store'] + read_gb * t['read']

for read_gb in (10, 500, 2000):          # 1,000 GB of exports, three read patterns
    costs = {tier: round(monthly(tier, 1000, read_gb), 2) for tier in TIERS}
    print(read_gb, 'GB read ->', costs, 'cheapest:', min(costs, key=costs.get))

# Expected output:
# 10 GB read -> {'hot': 20.0, 'cool': 10.1, 'cold': 4.3, 'archive': 1.2} cheapest: archive
# 500 GB read -> {'hot': 20.0, 'cool': 15.0, 'cold': 19.0, 'archive': 11.0} cheapest: archive
# 2000 GB read -> {'hot': 20.0, 'cool': 30.0, 'cold': 64.0, 'archive': 41.0} cheapest: hot

exercise.prompt: The notebook keeps learner exports for seven years. They are often downloaded in the first week, rarely after a month, and must be retrievable within a day if a learner asks. Design the storage account settings and lifecycle rules, and say what protects against accidental deletion.
exercise.solution: Store exports as blobs in a storage account with zone-redundant (or geo-zone-redundant, if a regional outage must be survived) redundancy. Upload to hot; a lifecycle rule moves blobs to cool after 30 days and to cold after 90 days. Archive is acceptable after a year only if standard rehydration fits inside the one-day retrieval requirement, otherwise keep them in cold. Delete after seven years with another rule. Enable blob soft delete and versioning (or an immutability policy if records must not be altered) because redundancy copies deletions too. Record metadata in the database so retrieval does not depend on listing.
checks: Chooses redundancy from the failures that must be survived.
Uses lifecycle rules that respect access pattern and minimum retention.
Checks the archive retrieval delay against the one-day requirement.
Protects against deletion with soft delete, versioning or immutability.

quiz.question: A storage account uses geo-redundant storage. A script deletes a container by mistake. What restores it?
options: Failing over to the secondary region
Soft delete, versioning or a separate backup enabled in advance
Nothing is needed; geo-redundancy keeps the deleted data
quiz.explanation: Replication copies the deletion. Only soft delete, versioning or an independent backup keeps the earlier data.

lessons.title: 6. Networks, DNS and traffic boundaries
lessons.takeaway: Connectivity requires routing, name resolution and permitted access.

sections.title: Routes, DNS and private endpoints
paragraphs: A virtual network provides address space and subnets for supported services. Routes determine where traffic goes; filters determine whether traffic is permitted; DNS resolves names. A private endpoint alone is not enough if the client resolves a public address or lacks access to the connected network. Overlapping address ranges complicate later peering.

sections.title: The inaccessible storage template
paragraphs: A training API calls private storage. Draw client, API, resolver and storage endpoint. Mark which paths are public, which are private and which identity authorizes data access. The supplied Azure storage template disables public networking and supplies no private endpoint, so it is intentionally not an accessible application backend.

quiz.question: Connectivity requires routing, name resolution and permitted access. Which decision follows?
options: Check DNS, network path and authorization as separate gates.
Assume private networking automatically grants permission to read data.
Create a private endpoint and assume every client automatically resolves and reaches it.
quiz.explanation: Network reachability and data authorization are independent controls.

references.scope: Azure networking overview; actual private connectivity also requires DNS and identity configuration.

exercise.prompt: In a Python prompt opened in the extracted kit, load topology.json, change resources[1]["public_network"] to True in memory, and call infra_lab.validate(resources). Predict the result. Then explain how wrong DNS differs from a reachable service denying an identity.
exercise.solution: validate raises ValueError because the model forbids public storage. The source JSON remains unchanged when only the loaded object changes. A wrong DNS result affects destination selection; a reachable service can still deny its data action. Neither local result proves Azure enforcement.
checks: Change an in-memory copy, leaving the source fixture intact.
Separate the local policy rejection from actual DNS and authorization behavior.

lessons.title: 7. Identity and least privilege
lessons.takeaway: Choose a principal, role and scope for each responsibility.

sections.title: RBAC scope and managed identity
paragraphs: Azure RBAC assignments combine principal, role definition and scope. Management-plane rights and supported data-plane rights are distinct. Roles are generally additive; a narrow assignment does not erase a broader assignment elsewhere. Managed identity can avoid stored client secrets for compatible Azure-hosted workloads, but local workstations do not automatically have that identity.

sections.title: Deployment versus runtime authority
paragraphs: The API needs to read one storage container, while the deployment identity creates a storage account in one resource group. These are different responsibilities and should not both receive subscription Owner. The optional template deliberately creates no role assignments because granting a real principal requires an explicit reviewed identity choice.

quiz.question: Choose a principal, role and scope for each responsibility. Which decision follows?
options: Grant separate narrowly scoped deployment and runtime permissions.
Give every component subscription Owner to avoid troubleshooting.
Add a resource-level Reader assignment and assume it removes an existing subscription Owner grant.
quiz.explanation: Least privilege and negative tests reduce impact while keeping distinct management and data responsibilities visible.

exercise.prompt: Write allowed and denied actions for deployment, API and reviewer. Include the broader-assignment check. Local policy tests exercise a simplified matrix, not Azure token acquisition or real RBAC enforcement.
checks: Separate deployment management rights from runtime data rights.
Include a broader/inherited-role check and denied example.
exercise.solution: The deployment identity can manage the isolated resource-group resources while the runtime identity gets only required data actions. Review broader inherited assignments because adding a narrow role does not remove wider rights. Test actual allowed/denied access in a separately chosen environment; the local matrix is only design evidence.

lessons.title: 8. Desired state and infrastructure as code
lessons.takeaway: Version configuration, inspect differences and review changes.

sections.title: Desired state and provider state
paragraphs: Infrastructure as code expresses desired resources and parameters so changes can be reviewed and reproduced. Terraform uses providers to interact with remote APIs and state to associate addresses with existing objects. Configuration is not the entire deployed system: manual drift, data contents and provider defaults also matter.

sections.title: The offline replacement model
paragraphs: Changing an owner tag should update metadata; changing a resource name may force replacement depending on provider schema. The offline planner models these cases using a small JSON inventory. It does not parse HCL or implement Terraform provider semantics.
Run Python snippets from the extracted practice folder with the supplied reference files. JSON fragments show the stated contract; they are not a complete deployment configuration.
sections.example:
from infra_lab import plan
import json
from pathlib import Path

desired = json.loads(Path('topology.json').read_text())['resources']
print(plan([], desired))  # create group; create store
print(plan(desired, desired))  # no-op for both

quiz.question: Version configuration, inspect differences and review changes. Which decision follows?
options: Review the difference between desired configuration, state association and real resources.
Treat committed JSON as proof the cloud already matches it.
Replace the state file with desired JSON and consider the remote resources reconciled.
quiz.explanation: Desired state becomes reality only through provider operations and observed verification.

lessons.title: 9. Providers, versions and initialization
lessons.takeaway: Pin compatible dependencies and verify the tool boundary.

sections.title: Core, providers and lock files
paragraphs: Terraform core and provider plugins evolve separately. `required_version` constrains core; `required_providers` identifies sources and version constraints. `terraform init` initializes the backend and obtains modules/providers. A dependency lock file records selected provider versions and checksums; a broad constraint alone does not reproduce an exact selection.

sections.title: Online initialization prerequisites
paragraphs: The Azure JSON template targets Terraform >=1.6 and <2 with AzureRM ~>4.0. That allows compatible 4.x provider selections; the learner must retain their generated lock file and record actual versions. Init needs internet or a configured plugin mirror; it is not an offline test.

quiz.question: Pin compatible dependencies and verify the tool boundary. Which decision follows?
options: Record actual tool versions and preserve the generated provider lock selection.
Assume a version constraint is the same as a committed lock file.
Delete the provider lock file before every release so all environments select their own newest version.
quiz.explanation: Constraints allow a range; the lock selection records the dependency actually chosen.

references.title: Terraform modules

exercise.prompt: Optional in a separate empty folder: copy main.tf.json, run terraform init -backend=false, then terraform validate. Record core and selected provider versions. No Azure apply is required and validation is not an account availability test.
checks: Record actual core and locked provider selections.
Distinguish dependency initialization from cloud provisioning and validation.
exercise.solution: Copy only the Azure template into a separate folder, initialize without a backend and validate using the selected provider. Record core and provider versions and preserve the generated lock selection. A compatible range can select different versions; initialization requires network/mirror and schema validation does not deploy or prove account availability.

lessons.title: 10. Variables, validation and outputs
lessons.takeaway: Define typed inputs and avoid secrets in state or examples.

sections.title: Input validation and sensitive outputs
paragraphs: Inputs let one configuration express several intentional environments. Use type constraints and validation for names, location and acceptable values. Outputs expose selected results, but marking a value sensitive masks presentation rather than encrypting state. Secrets can enter configuration, state, plans and logs; protect all of them.

sections.title: Names, tags and public identifiers
paragraphs: The template validates a lower-case storage name and requires `subscription_id` rather than using a hardcoded credential. Tags carry learning purpose and expiry. Outputting a storage account ID is different from outputting its keys; the teaching template exposes only the resource-group ID.

quiz.question: Define typed inputs and avoid secrets in state or examples. Which decision follows?
options: Validate public inputs and protect state even when values are marked sensitive.
Commit secrets after adding a sensitive=true display flag.
Output an access key marked sensitive and assume saved state no longer contains it.
quiz.explanation: Sensitive masking is not confidentiality for stored plans, state or repository history.

references.title: Terraform state

exercise.prompt: Compare a bad storage name containing hyphens with a valid lower-case alphanumeric one. Trace where a hypothetical connection secret could appear and choose a runtime secret-delivery mechanism instead of putting it in a sample variable file.
checks: Identify why a hyphenated name fails and a valid name passes.
Trace secret exposure beyond display masking.
exercise.solution: A hyphenated storage name fails the full template's lower-case alphanumeric 3-24 character validation. Explicit typed inputs are public configuration contracts. A sensitive flag masks output but secrets may remain in state, saved plans and logs; use an appropriate runtime identity/secret mechanism and protect those artifacts.

lessons.title: 11. Dependency graph and outputs
lessons.takeaway: References describe dependency without requiring a universal sequence.

sections.title: Expression-derived dependencies
paragraphs: Terraform derives dependencies from expressions that reference other resources. A storage account reference to a resource-group name establishes that relationship; independent resources may execute concurrently. `depends_on` can represent hidden dependencies but excessive blanket dependencies slow plans and make unknown values spread.

sections.title: The resource-group relationship
paragraphs: The template storage account uses the created resource-group name and location through references. The storage account depends on this resource group. Other resources may have different dependencies. A private endpoint would add further dependencies if intentionally designed.

quiz.question: References describe dependency without requiring a universal sequence. Which decision follows?
options: Use resource references for actual dependencies and avoid artificial total ordering.
Add depends_on from every resource to every other resource.
Serialize all resources with blanket depends_on to make every unknown value known before planning.
quiz.explanation: A dependency graph expresses necessary constraints; unrelated resources need not be serialized.

references.scope: Terraform 1.x module concepts; provider-specific schemas need validation.

references.title: Terraform on Azure overview
references.scope: Azure Terraform introduction; provider releases and resource availability remain changeable.

exercise.prompt: Inspect main.tf.json and draw only real dependencies. Distinguish a dependency edge from a request at runtime. Do not interpret the diagram as proof that the configured storage data endpoint is reachable.
checks: Draw only the resource reference relationships in the supplied template.
Distinguish dependency graph edges from runtime request sequence.
exercise.solution: The storage account references the group's name/location, establishing group-before-account; the selected output references the group's ID. These are configuration dependencies, not runtime storage calls. Independent resources can proceed concurrently. Private endpoint/DNS dependencies would need explicit design if added later.

lessons.title: 12. State, remote backends and locks
lessons.takeaway: State is sensitive coordination data, not an application backup.

sections.title: State identity, backups and locking
paragraphs: State maps Terraform addresses to remote resource identities and stores attributes. It can contain secrets. A remote backend can centralize access and versioning; locking depends on backend support. Application rows and blob contents require their own backups. Deleting state does not safely delete resources and can make future plans propose duplicates.

sections.title: Competing state writers
paragraphs: Two engineers applying different changes against separate state files can overwrite assumptions about the same real object. A shared lock-capable backend limits concurrent state writes, while protected state backups support recovery. The optional template uses local state unless the learner intentionally designs a remote backend.

quiz.question: State is sensitive coordination data, not an application backup. Which decision follows?
options: Protect shared state and handle active locks deliberately.
Delete the lock whenever a deployment appears slow.
Restore application rows by restoring only the Terraform state snapshot.
quiz.explanation: A live operation may still own the lock; bypassing it can permit conflicting state writes.

references.title: Terraform state
references.scope: Terraform 1.x language guidance; the offline inventory is a teaching model, not a Terraform state implementation.

references.title: Terraform state locking
references.scope: Lock support depends on backend; local lab tests no real distributed lock.

exercise.prompt: Describe state access, encryption, version recovery and lock ownership. Explain why force-unlock is only appropriate after confirming no live operation owns the lock. Do not commit *.tfstate, saved plans or credentials.
checks: Separate state recovery from application-data restoration.
Explain the active-owner check required before force-unlock.
exercise.solution: Protect state access, encryption and versioned recovery with a compatible lock-capable backend if collaborating. A lock owner may still be active even during a slow operation; force-unlock needs proof that no live owner remains. Application rows/blobs need separate backups. Local state in this optional template is not an automatically configured remote backend.

lessons.title: 13. Plan review and change classification
lessons.takeaway: A plan is a proposed operation set, not a successful deployment.

sections.title: Plan actions and unknown values
paragraphs: Read additions, in-place changes, replacements and deletions resource by resource. Some values remain unknown until apply. Check whether those unknown values affect access, data preservation or recovery. A saved plan contains sensitive information and can become inappropriate if surrounding conditions change. Review identity, scope, provider selection and destructive actions before applying.

sections.title: Simulated destructive changes
paragraphs: The offline planner replaces storage when its teaching identity name changes, and flags deletion when a desired ID is absent. It requires a separate `allow_destroy` argument for simulated destructive actions. This is a local policy contract, not Terraform replacement metadata.
sections.example:
from infra_lab import plan, simulate_apply
import json
from pathlib import Path

current = json.loads(Path('topology.json').read_text())['resources']
print(plan(current, []))  # two destroy operations in the MODEL
# simulate_apply(current, []) raises ValueError
print(simulate_apply(current, [], allow_destroy=True))  # []
# No cloud or filesystem resource is created/deleted.

sections.title: Read the action before reading the totals
paragraphs: Suppose a plan contains one tag update and one database replacement. The summary says two resources change, but only the replacement crosses the data-lifetime boundary. Read the address, before/after fields, action order and replacement reason. An unknown endpoint is normal during creation; an unknown backup destination is a missing recovery assumption. Neither observation is resolved by counting plus signs.

The optional `terraform_plan_drill.py` runs the real Terraform engine against its built-in `terraform_data` resource in a fresh temporary directory. An input-only edit plans an update; changing `triggers_replace` plans delete/create. Only the initial local state creation is applied. The `terraform_data` resource uses Terraform's built-in provider; no external provider plugin, provisioner or cloud resource is involved. These are real plan semantics, but they cannot predict which cloud-provider property forces replacement.
sections.example:
initial: [create], exit 2
after local apply: [no-op], exit 0
input v1 -> v2: [update], exit 2
identity-1 -> identity-2: [delete, create], exit 2

quiz.question: A plan is a proposed operation set, not a successful deployment. Which decision follows?
options: Review replacement and deletion effects, then verify after any separately chosen deployment.
Treat a successful plan as evidence that resources were created.
Treat every in-place update as operationally safe because it is not labeled destroy.
quiz.explanation: Planning predicts operations; only executed operations and observed results establish deployed state.

lessons.title: 14. Replacement and lifecycle safeguards
lessons.takeaway: Protect data across resource identity changes.

sections.title: Lifecycle protection and replacement
paragraphs: `create_before_destroy` can create a replacement first when the service permits coexistence, but unique naming and quotas can prevent that. `prevent_destroy` blocks certain configuration-driven destruction while present; removing the resource block also removes that protection. `ignore_changes` intentionally delegates selected drift and can conceal unexpected changes if used broadly.

sections.title: Data migration between accounts
paragraphs: Renaming a storage account is not equivalent to editing an owner tag. The provider may require a new account while data remains in the old one. The learner must copy and validate data, switch clients and retain recovery options rather than assuming replacement migrates contents.

quiz.question: Protect data across resource identity changes. Which decision follows?
options: Review replacement data movement and the limits of lifecycle guards.
Assume create_before_destroy automatically copies stored data.
Set ignore_changes on all attributes so future drift cannot threaten availability.
quiz.explanation: Lifecycle ordering manages resource operations; application data migration remains a separate task.

references.title: Terraform lifecycle
references.scope: Terraform lifecycle behavior, including limitations; no resource lifecycle operation is executed here.

exercise.prompt: Write a rename migration with copy verification, switch criterion and rollback deadline. Explain why deleting a resource block should still be reviewed even if prevent_destroy once appeared in it.
checks: Include copy verification, switch criterion and rollback deadline.
Describe the limits of create_before_destroy and removed prevent_destroy configuration.
exercise.solution: For storage rename, create a permitted new account, copy synthetic data with integrity checks, switch clients under an explicit criterion and retain rollback until the deadline. create_before_destroy does not copy data or bypass unique-name/quota constraints. Removing a block removes its prevent_destroy configuration; deletion still needs review.

lessons.title: 15. Modules and environment boundaries
lessons.takeaway: Reuse a contract without hiding ownership or mixing environments.

sections.title: Module contracts and environments
paragraphs: A module packages resources with typed inputs and outputs. Keep contracts small and avoid passing every provider field through without design. Development and production need distinct state, access and lifecycle policies. Terraform workspaces provide multiple states for one configuration but are not complete isolation of credentials, policy or organizational boundaries.

sections.title: A storage-module extension
paragraphs: A storage module could accept name, region and approved tags, and expose its ID. It should state networking prerequisites. The supplied template keeps the resource definitions in one file. Refactoring them into a module is an optional exercise.

quiz.question: Reuse a contract without hiding ownership or mixing environments. Which decision follows?
options: Separate reuse from access and state isolation.
Assume a workspace name alone prevents production access.
Embed production credentials in the reusable module so all environments share its behavior.
quiz.explanation: Workspace selection does not replace separate credentials, permissions and organizational controls.

references.scope: Terraform 1.x module concepts; provider-specific schemas need validation.

references.scope: Terraform 1.x language guidance; the offline inventory is a teaching model, not a Terraform state implementation.

checks: Define a small typed module contract and useful output.
Explain how a development runner is denied production identity/state access.
exercise.solution: A small storage module can accept approved name, region and tags and return its resource ID while documenting connectivity prerequisites. Development and production need distinct credentials, state permissions and lifecycle ownership. Reusing module source is compatible with isolation; workspace names alone cannot enforce that access boundary.

lessons.title: 16. Drift detection and adopting existing resources
lessons.takeaway: Import associates identity; review configuration before changing it.

sections.title: Drift and import ownership
paragraphs: Manual cloud changes can cause drift from configuration. A normal refreshed plan may propose restoring configured values. Decide whether an emergency change should be codified or reverted. Import associates an existing object with an address but does not automatically document every intended property or prove the next plan is safe.

sections.title: Public-access remediation
paragraphs: An operator temporarily enables public storage access during troubleshooting. The next plan should reveal the divergence; the security owner decides a controlled remediation. Importing an existing account needs exactly one intended state owner to avoid competing management.

sections.title: Separate observed state, desired configuration and ownership
paragraphs: Configuration says `public_access=false`, yesterday's state records false, and an operator changed the live account to true. Refresh reads the live value. A normal plan can then propose false because the configuration still specifies it. A refresh-only operation updates state without changing the remote account. Decide whether to add the emergency change to configuration or restore the original control.

Adopting an existing account adds a mapping between a Terraform address and the remote identity. If the configuration omits a required encryption or network property, the first post-import plan may propose an unexpected change. Compare the observed account, configuration and proposed actions before accepting management. Two state owners can each try to undo the other's changes; importing twice does not create high availability.
sections.example:
configuration: public_access=false
remote observation: public_access=true
normal plan: restore false
refresh-only: record true, do not remediate remote access

quiz.question: Import associates identity; review configuration before changing it. Which decision follows?
options: Review drift and adoption under a single explicit resource owner.
Import an existing object and apply immediately without inspecting the plan.
Manage the same imported resource from two state files to gain deployment redundancy.
quiz.explanation: State association is only the start of adoption; configuration can still propose destructive or unsafe changes.

references.scope: Import establishes a state association; adoption still requires configuration and a reviewed plan.

references.title: Terraform state
references.scope: Terraform 1.x language guidance; the offline inventory is a teaching model, not a Terraform state implementation.

exercise.prompt: An imported account has data and its first normal plan shows replacement because the configured name differs. What evidence would make adoption safe to continue?
checks: The differing name and replacement are identified before any apply.
The chosen action preserves existing identity/data or uses an explicit migration; importing alone is not called a backup.
exercise.solution: Stop before apply. Confirm the remote identity and intended owner, reconcile the name/configuration to the existing object when that is the goal, and review a fresh plan. If replacement is intentional, establish a separate tested migration and recovery path. Import associates identity; it neither copies data nor guarantees a harmless next plan.

lessons.title: 17. Policy checks and evidence limits
lessons.takeaway: Static checks catch selected mistakes without proving real enforcement.

sections.title: Policy checks and enforcement
paragraphs: Policy checks can reject missing owner/expiry tags, public endpoints or overbroad roles. Such checks are useful before a plan but can be bypassed if the real deployment path ignores them. Full authorization and network enforcement require tests against actual services. A locally passing JSON contract is evidence about that JSON only.

sections.title: The offline topology validator
paragraphs: `infra_lab.py` rejects public storage, wildcard roles and incomplete metadata in `topology.json`. It does not inspect an Azure tenant or enforce Azure Policy. The Azure template disables public networking but does not provide a complete private application network.
sections.example:
from infra_lab import validate
import json
from pathlib import Path

resources = json.loads(Path('topology.json').read_text())['resources']
resources[1]['public_network'] = True
try:
    validate(resources)
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)  # public storage forbidden by training policy

options: Combine static policies with actual enforcement tests at the target boundary.
Claim the real cloud is secure after mock policy tests pass.
Assume a local policy result prevents manual portal changes made by another authorized user.
quiz.explanation: Selected fixture checks cannot establish account configuration or live enforcement.

lessons.title: 18. Secret lifecycle and workload identity
lessons.takeaway: Reduce credential storage and test rotation and revocation.

sections.title: Federated and workload identities
paragraphs: Prefer short-lived or federated identity where supported. Managed identity is for compatible Azure-hosted resources; local developer login and CI federation have different flows. Do not print credentials in CI logs or embed them in Terraform examples. Secret rotation should include consumers, overlapping validity where needed and proof that revoked credentials fail.

sections.title: CI versus application credentials
paragraphs: A CI deployment exchanges a trusted workflow identity for a narrow Azure identity, while an application uses its own runtime identity. These identities must not be interchangeable. The optional template accepts no password or client secret and performs no real authentication in the offline lab.

quiz.question: Reduce credential storage and test rotation and revocation. Which decision follows?
options: Use distinct short-lived deployment and runtime identities with revocation tests.
Reuse one long-lived secret across developers, CI and the application.
Revoke a secret in a worksheet and assume all existing sessions and cached tokens instantly stop working.
quiz.explanation: Separate identities improve attribution, expiry control and the scope of compromised access.

lessons.title: 19. Cost estimation, budgets and cleanup
lessons.takeaway: Budget alerts are not automatic spending caps.

sections.title: Cost categories and budgets
paragraphs: Include compute uptime, storage, transactions, egress, monitoring retention and idle resources in estimates. Provider prices vary by region and date, so use the current calculator when considering real spend. Azure budgets can notify and connect automation but do not by themselves stop charges. Set an owner, expiry and teardown verification.

sections.title: Invented teaching rates
paragraphs: The offline model uses invented teaching rates: 2 units/hour times 10 hours plus 0.5 units/GB-month times 8 GB retained for one month equals 24 units. These are not Azure prices. A private endpoint or monitoring workspace can add costs beyond storage, and deleting compute may leave disks or addresses.
sections.example:
from infra_lab import estimate

print(estimate(2, 10, 0.5, 8))  # 24.0 fictional units
# compute: 2 units/hour * 10 hours = 20
# storage: 0.5 units/GB-month * 8 GB * 1 month = 4
# Not Azure pricing or a bill forecast.

quiz.question: Budget alerts are not automatic spending caps. Which decision follows?
options: Track all cost categories and verify resource removal instead of relying on alerts.
Assume an Azure budget automatically prevents overspending.
Set an expires tag and assume Azure automatically deletes the resources on that date.
quiz.explanation: A budget is a monitoring and notification mechanism unless separately integrated with controlled automation.

references.scope: Budgets notify and can integrate automation; a budget by itself does not cap or stop resource spending.

checks: Compute 24 fictional units without labeling them Azure prices.
Name cost categories, alert owner and observed cleanup checks.
exercise.solution: The invented teaching estimate is 20 compute units plus 4 storage units, total 24. Real review includes current regional compute, storage, transactions, egress, monitoring and idle costs. A budget needs an alert owner and response plan; it does not cap spending. Set expiry and verify teardown inventory instead of relying on tags alone.

lessons.title: 20. Autoscale, and map the services across clouds
lessons.takeaway: Autoscaling adds capacity from a measured signal within limits you set; scale out quickly, scale in cautiously, and recognise the same building blocks under AWS and Google Cloud names.

sections.title: Scaling rules
paragraphs: Autoscaling changes the number of instances (horizontal) rather than their size (vertical, which usually needs a restart). A rule needs a signal that tracks load: CPU, request rate, queue length or a custom metric. Target tracking computes the instance count that would bring the metric back to its target. Set a minimum for availability and cold starts, and a maximum that protects your budget (lesson 19) and the database behind the service.

Scale out fast and scale in slowly. New instances take time to start and warm up, and removing capacity on a brief dip causes flapping. Instances must be stateless and handle shutdown signals, finishing in-flight work, because the platform removes them without notice to users. Queue-based scaling (Container Apps and KEDA rules, for example) scales on backlog rather than CPU, which suits workers.

Try it: run the lab, then select Edit. The lab works from demand, so CPU falls as replicas are added; while every replica is at 100% the true demand is hidden and scale-out takes several steps. Lower `TARGET_CPU`, shorten `SCALE_IN_WAIT` or add a spike to `DEMAND` and watch replicas over time.
sections.example:
import math

# Try it: change these, then run again.
MIN, MAX, TARGET_CPU = 2, 10, 60          # replicas and the target average CPU percentage
SCALE_IN_WAIT = 3                         # intervals of low load before removing replicas
DEMAND = [110, 190, 330, 420, 240, 170, 170, 170, 170]   # total work per minute, in % of one replica's CPU

def desired(replicas, cpu):
    return max(MIN, min(MAX, math.ceil(replicas * cpu / TARGET_CPU)))

replicas, calm = MIN, 0
for minute, demand in enumerate(DEMAND):
    cpu = min(100, demand / replicas)     # a saturated replica reports 100% and hides the rest
    want = desired(replicas, cpu)
    if want > replicas:                   # scale out at once
        replicas, calm = want, 0
    elif want < replicas:                 # scale in only after sustained low load
        calm += 1
        if calm >= SCALE_IN_WAIT:
            replicas, calm = want, 0
    else:
        calm = 0
    print(f'minute {minute}: cpu {cpu:.0f}% -> {replicas} replicas')

# Expected output:
# minute 0: cpu 55% -> 2 replicas
# minute 1: cpu 95% -> 4 replicas
# minute 2: cpu 82% -> 6 replicas
# minute 3: cpu 70% -> 7 replicas
# minute 4: cpu 34% -> 7 replicas
# minute 5: cpu 24% -> 7 replicas
# minute 6: cpu 24% -> 3 replicas
# minute 7: cpu 57% -> 3 replicas
# minute 8: cpu 57% -> 3 replicas

sections.title: The same concepts on AWS and Google Cloud
paragraphs: The building blocks recur across providers, with different names and defaults. Learn the concept, then check the provider's limits, pricing and identity model before assuming behaviour carries over.

Managed web platform         App Service                Elastic Beanstalk             App Engine
Serverless containers        Container Apps             App Runner, ECS on Fargate    Cloud Run
Functions                    Azure Functions            Lambda                        Cloud Run functions
Managed Kubernetes           AKS                        EKS                           GKE
Object storage               Blob Storage               S3                            Cloud Storage
Managed relational database  Azure SQL Database         RDS, Aurora                   Cloud SQL
Workload identity            Managed identities         IAM roles                     Service accounts
Hierarchy for governance     Management groups,         Organizations, OUs,           Organization, folders,
                             subscriptions              accounts                      projects

exercise.prompt: A queue worker in Container Apps processes export jobs that take up to 3 minutes each. During a campaign the queue grows to 5,000 messages and the database reaches its connection limit. Design the scaling rule and its limits, and explain how scale-in must behave.
exercise.solution: Scale on queue length (for example one replica per 20 waiting messages) rather than CPU, because backlog is the load signal for a worker. Set minimum 0 or 1 depending on start-up latency needs, and a maximum derived from the database: if each replica uses 5 connections and 100 are available for workers, cap at 20 replicas. Scale out promptly; scale in only after the queue stays short for several minutes. On scale-in, replicas receive a shutdown signal: stop taking new messages, finish or abandon the current one so it returns to the queue, and keep handlers idempotent because a message may be processed twice. Alert on queue age so a capped system is visible.
checks: Scales on backlog rather than CPU.
Derives the maximum from a downstream limit.
Handles shutdown so in-flight messages are not lost and are processed idempotently.

quiz.question: Why scale in more slowly than you scale out?
options: Removing instances costs more than adding them
Brief dips would otherwise remove capacity that is needed again moments later, causing flapping and cold starts
Platforms forbid fast scale-in
quiz.explanation: Adding capacity late hurts users; removing it early hurts them too. A sustained-calm window avoids oscillation.

lessons.title: 21. CI planning and reviewed deployment
lessons.takeaway: Separate untrusted validation from credentialed mutation.

sections.title: Validation, plan and promotion
paragraphs: Run formatting, validation and policy checks before using deployment credentials. Pull-request code may be untrusted, so it should not receive deployment secrets. Check the saved plan, source commit, environment and provider selection. Apply the reviewed code and configuration to the intended environment, with a defined rollback or recovery procedure.

sections.title: Trusted release identity
paragraphs: A pull request runs offline Python checks with no Azure identity. A trusted release job can obtain scoped identity and generate a target-specific plan, with protected review before deployment. The supplied kit has no CI cloud credentials or auto-apply pipeline.

quiz.question: Separate untrusted validation from credentialed mutation. Which decision follows?
options: Keep untrusted checks unprivileged and bind deployment to a reviewed artifact.
Expose cloud credentials to every PR so plan checks are convenient.
Approve only the plan summary while letting an unreviewed release script choose the actual account and resources.
quiz.explanation: Untrusted executable code must not gain the privilege to mutate a real environment or exfiltrate its identity.

lessons.title: 22. Infrastructure tests and mock boundaries
lessons.takeaway: Distinguish syntax, model, provider and deployed-service tests.

paragraphs: JSON parsing checks syntax. Offline model tests check selected arithmetic and policy invariants. `terraform validate` checks language and provider schema after initialization. A plan can consult cloud APIs. Terraform test may create real resources unless runs are explicitly planned or providers mocked with compatible versions. Deployed smoke tests examine actual endpoints and identities.

paragraphs: The supplied Python suite tests a local inventory model without a database. The optional init and validate commands check the AzureRM schema without applying the configuration. Mock Terraform tests are discussed as an extension requiring Terraform 1.7+; they do not establish real service reachability.

Assume terraform test is always safe and offline by default.
Treat Terraform validate as a test of current subscription permissions and resource name availability.
quiz.explanation: Terraform test can provision resources; explicit run and provider choices determine behavior and potential cost.

lessons.title: 23. Recovery, backups and failure domains
lessons.takeaway: Infrastructure reconstruction and data restoration are separate plans.

sections.title: Failure domains and data recovery
paragraphs: A region, zone, account or identity failure can affect different parts of a workload. Rebuilding infrastructure from code does not restore database rows or blob contents. Define recovery point and time objectives, protect backups separately, and rehearse restoration in an isolated environment and verify the restored synthetic data.

sections.title: Missing files and lost state
paragraphs: If an export file store is lost, Terraform can create another account but cannot invent its missing files. If state is lost while the cloud survives, preserve resource identity and adopt carefully rather than creating duplicates. A rollback can also fail if data migrations are incompatible.

quiz.question: Infrastructure reconstruction and data restoration are separate plans. Which decision follows?
options: Restore infrastructure identity and application data through separate verified steps.
Claim RPO is zero because configuration is committed to Git.
Reapply the same configuration after data deletion and assume the recreated account contains its previous blobs.
quiz.explanation: Git configuration preserves intended topology, not necessarily application state or completed writes.

lessons.title: 24. Teardown and leftover resources
lessons.takeaway: Deletion needs scope checks and post-deletion verification.

sections.title: Destroy plans and residual resources
paragraphs: Review destroy plans as carefully as creates. Confirm subscription and resource identity, preserve needed data, and inspect provider-dependent order and deletion protections. Destroy may fail partway, leave soft-deleted objects or retain resources outside the managed state. Cost and data-retention cleanup need observed verification, not merely a command exit.

sections.title: The isolated teardown sequence
paragraphs: The offline planner refuses destroy actions without an explicit opt-in; it never calls Azure. For an independently chosen isolated real lab, review `terraform plan -destroy` before any `terraform destroy`, then check the portal and remaining state. A resource group must contain only your disposable learning resources.

Assume a successful destroy means every related charge and copy of data is gone.

quiz.explanation: State ownership, soft deletion and external resources can leave costs or retained data beyond the managed deletion.

references.scope: Azure architecture guidance; mock checks do not establish production readiness.

references.title: Terraform tests
references.scope: Terraform testing can use real resources by default; mock provider support requires compatible Terraform, introduced in 1.7.

references.title: Azure budgets
references.scope: Budgets notify and can integrate automation; a budget by itself does not cap or stop resource spending.

exercise.prompt: Present a go/no-go decision with three unresolved risks and a concrete next experiment for each. Reject any claim based solely on a mock test when it requires actual network, identity, data or cost evidence.
checks: Bind each readiness claim to actual observed or explicitly missing evidence.
Provide three unresolved risks with a next experiment and decision trigger.
exercise.solution: Present an ADR and identity/network graph, protected state design, plan classification, data recovery, cost categories and verified-cleanup proposal. Record local executed tests, optional provider validation and unexecuted live claims separately. Three go/no-go risks can be denied-access evidence, restore integrity and private-connectivity checks, each with a concrete next experiment.

stages.title: Cloud responsibility and scope map
stages.description: Design a small hypothetical private notebook without creating resources.
exitCriteria: Every operational responsibility has an owner.
Network reachability and permission are distinct.
Current cloud prices are not invented.

project.title: Cloud responsibility and scope map
project.brief: Design a small hypothetical private notebook without creating resources.
requirements: Compare static and managed app responsibilities.
Name tenant, subscription, region and disposable scope.
List cost categories and data owners.
rubric: Every operational responsibility has an owner.
Network reachability and permission are distinct.
Current cloud prices are not invented.
project.solution: Retain static hosting until authenticated writes are needed. Map client/API/storage identities and routes, and choose an isolated learning scope with owner and expiry. Estimate categories, then consult current regional pricing before real spend.

project.title: Reviewed infrastructure plan
project.brief: Run the offline planner and inspect the optional Azure Terraform JSON.
requirements: Review typed inputs, state handling and dependencies.
Optionally init/validate in a separate empty folder; record results.
rubric: Model output is not presented as Terraform output.
Destruction and replacement include data consequences.
Provider validation is distinct from deployment.
project.solution: Use the teaching planner to prove its explicit policy and operation contract. The optional provider-backed template needs Terraform initialization, an actual locked AzureRM selection and validate; it does not provide private application connectivity or perform a deployment.

stages.title: Cloud launch and teardown review
stages.description: Prepare an evidence portfolio for a future full-stack deployment.
exitCriteria: No mock result becomes a real cloud claim.
State and application data recovery are separate.

project.title: Cloud launch and teardown review
project.brief: Prepare an evidence portfolio for a future full-stack deployment.
requirements: Separate PR checks from privileged release steps.
Design state, identity and data recovery.
Create cost, expiry and cleanup checklists.
Specify real denied-access, restore and smoke tests still needed.
rubric: No mock result becomes a real cloud claim.
State and application data recovery are separate.
project.solution: Review the exact resource graph and identity scopes, protected state and credential boundaries; rehearse data recovery in an independently chosen environment. Confirm budget alerts are not a cap. Scope-check and review every deletion, then verify retained objects and cost sources.
